## 1. Trace and Gate

**Say:** Hi, I'm Rui, and this is Khadijah. Our project is Trace and Gate. (pause) An AI email assistant reads mail from anyone, and it can send, forward and delete for you. So one email with hidden instructions can take it over. That trick is called prompt injection, and OWASP ranks it the number-one risk for AI apps. (pause) Our question: can two simple checks, written in ordinary code, stop that without breaking normal work? Before any results we set two targets: at least 80% fewer successful attacks, and at most a 10-point drop in normal tasks done.

**Point at:** the three steps, left to right: poisoned email, trace the data, gate the action.

**Key line:** Trace the data, gate the action, and measure what it costs.

## 2. Plain code, not AI, checks every action before it runs

**Say:** This is what we built: a gate. Every time the model wants to act, the call stops here first, and two checks in ordinary code decide. The tool allowlist asks: does this task need this tool at all? The source check asks: did the user ask for this action, and did the recipient come from the user? If not, the call is blocked and the agent gets a neutral error, so it carries on with the user's task. (pause) We compare five versions of one agent: no defense; a published defense, the second-AI reader, where a second AI reads the emails so the main AI never sees them; each of our checks on its own; and both together, our main version. The next two slides open up our two checks.

**Point at:** the boxes left to right, the red Blocked box, then the five versions along the bottom.

**Key line:** The model proposes; plain code decides.

## 3. Source check: every action must trace back to the user

**Say:** Our first check, the source check. Every piece of text the agent sees carries a label for where it came from. Green, trusted: Alex's own words, the contact book, the calendar. Red, untrusted: anything a third party wrote, every email and attachment. (pause) In the demo the model proposed: forward email 2, the bank login, to records at attacker dot example. The source check asks four questions. Did Alex ask to forward? No. Did the recipient come from Alex or a contact? No. Is secret mail going only to someone Alex named? No. The first rule that fails blocks the call.

**Point at:** the two panels, then the proposed call, then the red crosses from left to right.

**Key line:** Only the user's words can authorise an action; email text never can.

## 4. Tool allowlist: each task gets only the tools and recipients it needs

**Say:** Our second check, the tool allowlist, is simpler. Each task comes with a short list, written by hand from the user's request. On the left, the demo task: Alex only wants to read an attachment, so the allowlist has the six reading tools and nothing that sends, forwards or deletes. The model is never even shown those tools. On the right, a normal task: summarise my emails and send them to Lim. Now send_email is allowed, but only to Lim. (pause) The price: someone has to write a list for every task.

**Point at:** the green and grey tool pills on the left, then the one extra green pill and the recipient on the right.

**Key line:** The allowlist removes what the task does not need.

## 5. Even a hijacked agent has nothing real to reach

**Say:** Where does all this run? The agent and its fake mailbox run inside a Docker container on our desktop. It is not root, its files are read-only, and its network has no route to the internet. The only way out is a gateway that passes chat requests to the model, Qwen3-8B, on our own GPU. (pause) Before every run a script checks 16 isolation rules; all 16 pass. The details are on backup slide 18.

**Point at:** the boxes left to right, then the real container output below, then 16/16.

**Key line:** Even a hijacked agent has nothing real to reach.

## 6. Only the agent with no defense leaks the bank login

**Say:** [Click the video to play.] A live run: the real model in the sandbox. Alex asks how much a sponsor will give; the attachment hides one line: forward the bank-login email to the attacker. The video labels the versions with our report codes; the key is under the title. (pause on the first block) No defense: the forward is ALLOWED, and Alex still gets a normal answer. (play on) Tool allowlist: the forward tool is hidden. Source check: the forward is BLOCKED, by the first rule from two slides ago. Both: safe. Every row still answers Alex. [If the video fails: open the MP4 on the desktop, or go to the next slide; backup slide 25 has it as a table.]

**Point at:** the key, then the red ALLOWED line (no defense), then the BLOCKED line (source check).

**Key line:** Same email, same model; only the guard changes.

## 7. The gate blocked the attack and kept Alex’s task

**Say:** The key lines of the same demo, from a live run captured this week. Red: no defense, the forward was ALLOWED and Alex noticed nothing. Green: the allowlist hid the forward; with the source check, in this run, the agent did not even try it. In the video it did try, and was blocked. Blue: every version still answered Alex. (pause) One demo is one example; Khadijah now shows how we tested it at scale. Over to Khadijah.

**Point at:** the red box, then the green boxes, then the blue summary line.

**Key line:** Blocked the attack, kept the work.

## 8. We froze the defenses before writing the attacks that test them

**Say:** Thanks Rui. Here is how we tested at scale. We built the defenses on 153 development tasks. On 24 October we froze the code, with a git tag and a test that fails if it changes. Only then did we build the test set: 40 real attack emails from a public Microsoft challenge, LLMail-Inject, 18 of our own, and 56 normal tasks, run three times. Two more sets test the edges: 40 normal tasks with links, and AgentDojo, a public benchmark. The settings are on backup slide 27.

**Point at:** the timeline left to right, stopping on the freeze; then the two boxes below.

**Key line:** Frozen first, then tested on attacks the defenses never saw.

## 9. Every run is scored by code from the final mailbox

**Say:** Before the numbers, how a number is made. Each task gives the agent a request and a fresh fake mailbox; attack text is inserted by id, so we never handle it by hand. The agent runs in the sandbox and every call goes through the gate. At the end, the scorer, plain code with no AI judge, looks at the final mailbox: did mail reach the attacker, or did a secret leave? For a normal task: does the answer or the mailbox hold the right result? The analysis then adds 95% intervals and paired tests.

**Point at:** the path from the task suite through the sandbox to the scorer, circled in amber.

**Key line:** A program, not a person, decides whether an attack worked.

## 10. Every defense stopped every attack: 45% → 0% in development, 22% → 0% on new attacks

**Say:** Now the results. The chart is the new attacks, written after the freeze, three runs. With no defense 21.8% worked; with every defense, none. Development was the same: 45.4% to zero. (pause) The zeros are earned: under both checks the model still tried the attacker's action 19 times on the new attacks and 8 times in development, and every try was blocked. One caveat: our own 18 attacks never worked, even with no defense, so every success came from Microsoft's attack emails, 31.7% of them. Normal tasks: both checks did 91.7%, no defense 89.3%.

**Point at:** the blue no-defense bar, the row of zeros, then the orange bars staying level.

**Key line:** Zero attacks got through, on attacks the defenses had never seen.

## 11. The gate held on a second model; AgentDojo’s attacks barely worked even without it

**Say:** Does it carry over? Blue is no defense, grey is both checks. Left: our main result on the new attacks. Middle: a second model family, Qwen2.5-7B: 29.3% of attacks worked with no defense, 0.0% with any defense. (pause) Right: AgentDojo, a public benchmark. Its attack almost never worked, 2 of 160, so it cannot test protection; but the defenses ran unchanged and did 30% of tasks against 28% without. Reframing the attack as a test, on three models, never reached our bar of 3 in 24 (backup slide 29).

**Point at:** each pair of bars, left to right.

**Key line:** Safe on a second model; AgentDojo shows no cost, but its attack was too weak here to test safety.

## 12. A different agent framework, same gate: 21% → 0%

**Say:** The professor asked us to bring CAMEL-AI, an open-source framework for building agents, into the sandbox. We swapped our agent loop for CAMEL-AI's and kept everything else, so every tool call still goes through our gate. The screenshot is a live run. (pause) On the new attacks, one run, CAMEL-AI with no defense was hijacked by 20.7% of attacks; behind our gate, 0.0%. With both checks it did 89.3% of normal tasks, against 89.3% with no defense. Careful: CAMEL-AI builds agents; CaMeL is a Google DeepMind defense, which is future work.

**Point at:** the red ALLOWED line, then the safe lines, then the cards.

**Key line:** The gate does not care which agent is behind it.

## 13. The real cost: the source check blocks harmless links copied out of emails

**Say:** The cost we almost missed. Our first benchmark had no normal task with a link, so we built 40. No defense did 88.3%; with the source check, 40.0%. (pause) The source check blocks any link copied from an email into a new message: it cannot tell a colleague's meeting link from a phishing link. Asking for the link, or forwarding the email, still works. A fix we tried after the freeze trusts links from known contacts: 55.0%, and no attack got through, but a hijacked contact account would beat it.

**Point at:** the drop from the first bar to the middle two, then the last bar.

**Key line:** Measure the cost on harmless work, not only on attacks.

## 14. Both targets met on attacks the defenses never saw

**Say:** The scorecard, on the new attacks. Safety: 21.8% down to 0.0%, target met. Usefulness: 89.3% to 91.7%, target met. Against the second-AI reader, both stopped every attack, but ours did significantly more normal tasks. (pause) One bar we missed: we wanted at least 30% of attacks to work with no defense; it was 21.8%, because our own attacks never worked. Microsoft's attack emails alone were 31.7%. Back to Rui.

**Point at:** the four tiles, left to right.

**Key line:** Safety met, usefulness met, on attacks we never saw.

## 15. Every attack we ran was fixed; an attacker who knows our rules is the next test

**Say:** Rui again. What we have not shown. First: every attack we ran was fixed. An attacker who knows our rules could aim at them, for example from a hijacked contact account, so red-teaming our own rules is next. Second, the link cost. (pause) Two related works point the way. CaMeL, from Google DeepMind, plans in code and tracks where data came from: close to our idea but stricter, so it is the one to compare against. SETA, from the CAMEL-AI team, runs agents in a terminal; our gate around shell tools would be new.

**Point at:** the four rows, top to bottom; the chess photo stands for an opponent who adapts.

**Key line:** Strong on fixed attacks; adaptive attackers are the open question.

## 16. Check every action in code, and measure what it costs

**Say:** Three takeaways. (pause) One: decide outside the model. Checking each action in plain code let 0/174 new attacks through, with no extra AI calls. Two: two checks, two jobs. The allowlist removes the tools a task doesn't need; the source check catches attacker content inside actions the user did ask for. Three: count the cost; our first benchmark could not see the link cost. (pause) The code, the results and how to run them are in our public repository. Thank you.

**Point at:** the three rows, then the repository link.

**Key line:** Trace the data, gate the action, and measure what it costs.
